<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="PubMed-not-MEDLINE" Owner="NLM"><PMID Version="1">42924073</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>2026</Year><Month>10</Month><Day>24</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2026</Year><Month>10</Month><Day>24</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Electronic-eCollection"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Print">1662-680X</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Print"><Volume>18</Volume><Issue>1</Issue><PubDate><Year>2026</Year><Season>Jan-Dec</Season></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Case reports in neurology</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Case Rep Neurol</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Bilateral Foot Drop as the Presenting Manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus-Associated Mononeuritis Multiplex: A Case Report.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>567</StartPage><EndPage>579</EndPage><MedlinePgn>567-579</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1159/crn/abyag002</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="INTRODUCTION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Peripheral nervous system involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is uncommon, and mononeuritis multiplex as the presenting neurological manifestation is particularly rare. Early recognition may be difficult when the initial clinical picture resembles focal compressive neuropathy.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CASE PRESENTATION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">A 31-year-old previously healthy woman developed acute right foot numbness and foot drop after right knee pain and earlier nonspecific arthralgia. Initial assessments favored peroneal neurapraxia. Over the following 3 weeks, her deficits progressed to persistent right foot drop followed by new left lower limb numbness and weakness, resulting in asymmetric bilateral foot drop. Electrophysiological studies demonstrated an asymmetric, non-length-dependent motor and sensory axonal neuropathy consistent with mononeuritis multiplex. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine excluded a compressive lumbosacral explanation and focused ultrasound showed no compressive lesion involving the right common peroneal nerve. Serological evaluation revealed high-titer antinuclear antibody, positive anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-Ro, anti-ribosomal P antibodies, elevated inflammatory markers, and a positive lupus anticoagulant screen, with negative infectious screening and no evidence of active lupus nephritis. She was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, intravenous immunoglobulin, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab, followed by oral corticosteroid tapering and rehabilitation. Her pain improved early, distal motor function partially recovered, and she later demonstrated meaningful functional improvement with orthotic and rehabilitation support.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">This case suggests that SLE may initially present predominantly as mononeuritis multiplex, with evolving bilateral foot drop as the dominant neurological and function-threatening manifestation, through a suspected vasculitic mechanism, even when more typical renal, serosal, or major mucocutaneous features are absent at neurological presentation. In patients with progressive or sequential foot drop, especially when the presentation becomes bilateral or multifocal, prompt electrodiagnostic testing and evaluation for systemic autoimmune disease are essential to avoid diagnostic delay and allow timely immunotherapy.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026. Neurol</MedlineTA><NlmUniqueID>101517693</NlmUniqueID><ISSNLinking>1662-680X</ISSNLinking></MedlineJournalInfo><OtherAbstract Type="plain-language-summary" Language="eng"><AbstractText>Foot drop means difficulty lifting the front part of the foot, which can cause tripping or an abnormal walking pattern. It is often caused by pressure on a nerve near the knee or by a problem in the lower back. This case describes a 31-year-old woman who first developed numbness and weakness in her right foot. At first, her symptoms looked similar to a common nerve compression problem. Over the next few weeks, she developed symptoms in both legs. Nerve tests showed that several separate nerves were affected. This pattern is called mononeuritis multiplex. Blood tests also supported a new diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease in which the immune system can attack the body’s own tissues. In this patient, the nerve problem was considered most likely related to lupus-associated inflammation of the small blood vessels that supply the nerves, although this was not confirmed by nerve biopsy. She was treated with medicines to reduce immune system activity, including steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab. She also received physiotherapy and ankle-foot supports to improve walking. Her pain and movement improved, although some weakness remained during follow-up. This case highlights that worsening or bilateral foot drop should not always be assumed to be due to simple nerve compression. When symptoms progress or affect both sides, doctors should consider inflammatory and autoimmune causes and arrange appropriate nerve and blood tests.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026.
